summary: Many applications secure connections with TLS and X.509 certificates. This document specifies procedures for representing and verifying the identity of application services in those interactions: how a client checks that the certificate matches the server it meant to reach. It obsoletes RFC 6125.

eli5.summary: When you call a shop you check the name on the ID matches the one you meant to call. This explains how computers do that check.

subtitle: How a TLS client checks that the certificate a server presents really names the service it meant to reach.

tldr.problem: A client that connects over TLS must be sure that the certificate belongs to the service it intended to reach, or the encryption protects a conversation with the wrong party.
tldr.mechanism: The client builds its own list of reference identifiers, then compares them with the identifiers in the certificate's subjectAltName extension: DNS names, IP addresses, SRV names or URIs. The Common Name is never used.
tldr.outcome: A match gives the client a validated identity, and no match must end the connection with a bad certificate error. RFC 9525 obsoletes RFC 6125.

facts.label: Wildcards per name
facts.value: One, as the whole left-most label

today: RFC 9525 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2023 and has not been obsoleted. It obsoletes RFC 6125, so it is the current definition of service identity checks for TLS.

sections.title: Why Service Identity Needs Rules
sections.content:
When a client talks to an application service over TLS, DTLS or a protocol built on them such as QUIC, it has some idea of who the server is, for example 'the website at bigcompany.example'. The server presents its own idea of its identity in a public key certificate issued by a certification authority under the Internet PKI using X.509. The RFC calls these the client's reference identity and the server's presented identity. The client must check that they match so that it can authenticate the connection automatically.

RFC 9525 defines how clients do this check. It therefore also puts requirements on certification authorities, on administrators who request certificates and on designers of application protocols. It obsoletes RFC 6125.

It does not replace the certificate issuance and validation rules in the PKIX profile. It addresses only name forms in the end-entity server certificate, so applications still need to verify the whole certification path.
sections.eli5: Before you trust someone at the door, you check their badge says the name you were expecting. This document is the list of rules for reading the badge.

sections.title: Scope and Summary of the Rules
sections.content:
The rules apply to service identities used in TLS or DTLS and carried in PKIX certificates. That covers protocols that reuse the TLS handshake with a different record layer, with QUIC as the prominent example. They also apply to credentials derived from such certificates, such as delegated credentials.

Out of scope are client or end-user identities, certification authority policies, how DNS names are resolved, and user interface issues.

The introduction summarizes the main rules:

  • Check DNS domain names only through the dNSName entry of the subjectAltName extension.
  • More specific entries are allowed where appropriate: uniformResourceIdentifier, iPAddress and the otherName form SRVName.
  • Wildcards are now supported by default, but only as the complete left-most label.
  • Do not include or check domain-like strings in the subject's Common Name.
sections.eli5: The rules cover the badge's name and nothing else: not the badge maker's rules, not how you found the address, and not what the door looks like.

sections.title: Identifiers and Their Types
sections.content:
An application service is identified by a DNS domain name, an IP address, or an identifier carrying extra information, namely the application service type from a DNS SRV record or a URI. Four identifier types live in the subjectAltName extension.

  • DNS-ID: an entry of type dNSName.
  • IP-ID: an entry of type iPAddress, a 4-octet IPv4 or 16-octet IPv6 address.
  • SRV-ID: an otherName entry of the SRVName form, such as _imap.isp.example.
  • URI-ID: an entry of type uniformResourceIdentifier.

Identifiers are either direct (typed in or configured by a person) or indirect (resolved automatically, as with SRV). They are either unrestricted (usable for any service) or restricted (usable for one type of service). A DNS-ID and an IP-ID are direct and unrestricted, an SRV-ID is typically indirect and restricted, and a URI-ID is direct and restricted. Sharing one certificate between services invites cross-protocol attacks such as ALPACA, and restricted identifiers or separate certificates are the remedy.

The Common Name RDN MUST NOT be used to identify a service, because it is free-form text and therefore ambiguous. Other RDNs in the subject name MUST NOT be used either. Internationalized domain labels are written as A-labels, and only US-ASCII characters are allowed in a DNS-ID.
sections.eli5: A badge can show a name, a number or a job title. The rules say which parts you may read, and they say never to trust the scribbled nickname on the front.

sections.title: Rules for Issuers, Requesters and Protocol Designers
sections.content:
A certificate MUST include at least one identifier and SHOULD include a DNS-ID as a baseline for interoperability. If the technology's specification calls for SRV-IDs, as XMPP does, or URI-IDs, as SIP does, the certificate SHOULD include them too. A certificate MAY hold several identifiers of each kind and MAY carry other application-specific identifiers for compatibility, which are out of scope. For a URI-ID, the scheme MUST be that of the application protocol, and the host component MUST be the service's FQDN.

Service providers asking for a certificate SHOULD request as few identifiers as needed to identify a single service. If the certificate will be used for only one type of service, they SHOULD request a DNS-ID or IP-ID, or an SRV-ID or URI-ID that limits the certificate to that type. If it may be used for any service, they SHOULD request only DNS-IDs or IP-IDs, although the RFC discourages this because of multiprotocol attacks.

Protocol designers should reference this document normatively. A specification MAY allow only one identifier type. If it does not use SRV records or URIs for services, it MUST say that SRV-ID or URI-ID is not supported, and it MAY disallow wildcards, in which case it MUST state that wildcard certificates are not supported.
sections.eli5: The people who make badges, the people who ask for them and the people who write the club rules each get a short list of things they should and should not put on a badge.

sections.title: Verifying Service Identity
sections.content:
The check runs in three steps: the client builds a list of reference identifiers, the server presents its identifiers in a certificate, and the client compares them. The client MUST build its list independently of what the server presents. The inputs can be a typed URL, configured account details or a hyperlink. Intermediate names met during DNS resolution are not reference identifiers and MUST NOT be treated as such.

The identifier type depends on the service. If a service is typically tied to URIs for security, the reference SHOULD be a URI-ID. If it is typically found through SRV records, it SHOULD be an SRV-ID. An IP address gives an IP-ID, and otherwise a DNS-ID is used. Local policy decides which types a client accepts.

Matching works like this:

  • DNS names are compared label by label, case-insensitively as ASCII. Internationalized names are first converted from U-labels to A-labels.
  • A wildcard is honored only if the presented identifier has a single asterisk that is the complete left-most label. Otherwise that identifier is invalid and MUST be ignored. A wildcard matches exactly one label.
  • An IP-ID must match the iPAddress entry octet for octet, with no network-level matching.
  • For SRV-IDs and URI-IDs, the service name or scheme MUST also match, case-insensitively, but only against the domain from that same identifier.

If a match is found, the client MUST use the matched reference identifier as the validated identity. If none is found, an automated client SHOULD end the attempt with a bad certificate error and log it, and it MUST NOT disable this by default. A client controlled by a person SHOULD tell the user and end the attempt, though it MAY let advanced users proceed with great caution.
sections.eli5: You write down the names you would accept before you look at the badge. Then you compare letter by letter, and if nothing matches, you do not go in.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists the risks that remain even when matching is done correctly.

  • Wildcards vouch for any single-label host in their domain, which is convenient but can cover rogue or buggy hosts. Limiting them to one wildcard in the left-most label helps. Protecting against wildcards on public suffixes such as *.com is beyond the scope of the document, and protocols can disallow wildcards altogether.
  • IP addresses: the TLS Server Name Indication extension carries only domain names, so a server wanting to present an IP-ID must do so when a connection arrives without SNI. The text form of an IPv4 address can also be misread as a domain name, so identifiers should be classified consistently.
  • Multiple identifiers: a certificate with many names is only as strong as the weakest server that offers those names.
  • Name constraints on a CA cover only the name forms listed, so a CA constrained for DNS-IDs is not automatically constrained for SRV-IDs or URI-IDs.
  • Trust: the document assumes a trusted CA's certificates are all trusted, and checks for bad behavior by the named hosts belong to the application.

The RFC also says that matching internationalized names on A-labels limits confusion over look-alike characters, though such concerns belong to applications and user interfaces.
sections.eli5: Even a perfect badge check can be fooled if one badge works for many doors or the badge maker is careless, so the rules warn you to keep badges narrow.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 6125
sections.content:
RFC 9525 revises RFC 6125 after about a decade of experience. The main changes are:

  • A wildcard can appear only as the complete left-most label.
  • Server identity can be expressed only in the subjectAltName extension. Using the commonName, known as CN-ID in RFC 6125, is no longer valid.
  • The long discussion of pinning was replaced by two paragraphs in the outcome section.
  • IP-ID reference identifiers were added.
  • More text on multiple identifiers and their security considerations was added.
  • The material on target audiences, the X.500 directory, the survey of prior art and the sample text was removed.
  • The title was shortened because the old one was hard to cite.
sections.eli5: This is the updated rule book. It no longer lets you read the scribbled nickname, and it adds a way to read numeric addresses.
